title: Push/Pull Pull/Legs Legs/Push 3 days program review
summary: NH reviews a subscriber's 3-day hypertrophy program (Push/Pull, Pull/Legs, Legs/Push), mostly dumbbell-based. He critiques day pairings, rep ranges and set counts, and proposes supersets and giant sets to save time, swapping lat pulldowns for weighted pull-ups, adding a trap bar deadlift on the pull/legs day, and dropping supinated barbell rows.

claims.claim: Pull and legs pair well on one day because the deadlift involves the legs while also being a pull.
Doing push and pull on the same day pairs antagonist muscles and isn't synergistic; that's why push/pull/legs separates them.
Legs and push can work together somewhat because overhead and push presses use the legs to stabilize or drive the weight.
Simple double progression (reach the top of the rep range, add weight, start over) is what he uses too; progression schemes matter less than rep and set schemes.
He dislikes rotating an exercise whenever you stall on it, because letting failure trigger the change is bad for mental strength.
Recovery speed differs by muscle across people, but there are individual differences: his triceps recover very fast while his quads take forever.
The upper back recovers very quickly compared with other muscles.
He has a personal bias against unilateral movements, but admits they help bring up a weak side or imbalances.
A program review is easier when the lifter states clear goals, such as not wanting to grow the legs.
Horizontal presses pair well with rows, and vertical presses with vertical pulls, but such a superset should be part of a day, not define its whole emphasis.
He likes an evolving rep range such as 3x6-8 for dumbbell bench as strength work.
Weighted pull-ups beat lat pulldowns: you move your body through space, the stretch isn't limited by machine hinges, and machine resistance curves are inconsistent.
On heavy pulldowns the thigh pad holds you down so the spine gets stretched, and many machines put the handle in front, turning it into a rear-delt pull rather than a lat stretch.
With a 10-15 rep range you should do 4 sets rather than 3; if reps crash from 15 to 13 across sets you're either not pushing hard enough or chose the wrong weight.

Face pulls shouldn't be loaded heavily or limited by mechanical failure; if your torso can't stay vertical the weight is too heavy. Do them for 4 sets of 8-12 (or 10-15), limited by the traps and rear delts.
At the end of a workout, 3 sets of 10-15 on cable flies is fine: reps dropping from 15 to 12 is logical when the muscle is burnt out, and it's a safe movement to push to failure on.
With only one curl movement in the session, do 4 sets of 8-12 instead of 3; extra biceps volume can't hurt.
Superset antagonist movements like dumbbell bench with pull-ups: it won't hurt performance, only cardiovascular capacity, so take a short rest between the two.
Supersets save time, raise metabolic demand and keep you efficient; they're always worth chasing.
Finish a workout with a giant set of three isolation movements done back to back with no rest.
Keep the last heavy compound of a session unsupersetted so you can put all your remaining strength into it.
You don't need a barbell to make gains; it helps but isn't required.
Supinated-grip bent-over rows are dangerous because they risk overstretching the biceps; if you do them, use 4 sets of 10-12 rather than 3x6-8 so you control the weight.
He doesn't like leg curls or leg extensions much and would rather see squats, but they're fine if they don't aggravate your knees.
If you do lat pulldowns, do them with a V-bar to the stomach; lean back and drive the elbows in to keep the lats engaged instead of using the arms.
Supinated inverted rows are one of the few safe supinated row options.
4x8-12 is a good shrug prescription; 10-15 also works.

Evolving rep ranges let you control volume but are a double-edged sword: the freedom can mess with your head, so you have to track that tonnage never drops. Fixed rep ranges are constant, so only the weight changes.
Open a pull/legs day with trap bar deadlifts: it builds strength and size and warms the body up.
Supersets are trickier on lower body days because leg lifts are very taxing on the cardiovascular system and it's easy to overreach.
3x6-8 on squats is enough to maintain legs if you don't want to grow them.
Squats followed by bench means re-warming up, and blood (the pump) keeps switching areas, so he doesn't find legs/push synergistic.
When a lift is trained heavy twice a week, make one day volume-focused (e.g. 4x8-12) and the other heavy (3x6-8).
Too many horizontal presses and too few overhead presses can cause shoulder impingement and imbalances; incline bench doesn't replace the overhead press. Do 4x8-12 or 4x10-15 on the standing press.
Placing the most taxing day (four heavy compounds) right before the weekend is smart, since you get two days to eat and sleep.
Never superset heavy squats, heavy bench, RDLs or standing press; you need to be fresh for them.
After heavy compounds you're burnt out and won't give isolation work your all, so put the isolation movements into one giant set for a full-body pump.
Putting pull/legs days between push days is smart if your triceps recover slowly.

cues: move your body around the bar
exercises.why: better lat stretch and more aesthetic than machine pulldowns

exercises.why: criticised: inconsistent machine tension, spine stretched by thigh pad, handle position makes it a rear-delt pull

exercises.name: V-bar lat pulldown
cues: pull elbows in to engage lats

exercises.name: Face pull
cues: limited by traps and rear delts, not mechanical failure

exercises.why: safe to push to failure at the end of a session

exercises.name: Supinated bent-over row
exercises.why: criticised as dangerous for the biceps

exercises.why: open the pull/legs day for strength, size and warm-up

exercises.why: more overhead volume to balance horizontal pressing and prevent impingement
